## Redact: secrets kept out of the Nix store

> **Last verified:** 2026-10-24 — consumers can test exact references through
> the public predicate before extracting their file paths.

`lib/redact` is a pure `{lib}` import, exported as `lib.redact`. A value either
is cleartext, which is visible and lands in the store, or names where a secret
lives. Nothing is read at evaluation. The reader resolves each reference when a
launcher starts.

### References

`redact.file "/run/secrets/x"` and `redact.command "/abs/program"` return the
markers `{_redact.file = path;}` and `{_redact.command = path;}`.
`redact.concat ["Bearer " ref]` holds literal strings and references, for a
header prefix or a token inside a URL. MCP consumers use it for composed URLs
and headers. A concat needs at least one reference and cannot nest.

A path must be an absolute string without an empty, `.` or `..` segment. A file
path must also have no string context: `./secret` and `"${./secret}"` have
already copied the file into the world-readable store, so both are refused. A
file path under `builtins.storeDir` is refused whatever its context, so a
context-free `toString ./secret` from a flake is refused too. The test is
lexical: a symlink that leads into the store is not resolved.

A command takes neither test, because the program is code and its output is the
value. `redact.command "${pkgs.x}/bin/x"` is the normal form: its context
carries into the launcher `assign` writes, so the program stays a runtime
dependency of that launcher. Nothing checks what a program contains, so a script
that embeds a secret is not caught.

The marker shape is the only representation. `isMarker`, `isReference`,
`isConcat`, `isRedacted` and `isAsFile` in `default.nix` are the one copy of
that logic. Constructors, types and `assign` all reach it through `sealed`.
`isAsFile`, `isPath`, `isRedacted`, `isReference`, `isReserved` and `sealed` are
exported, so a consumer that walks values (`lib/extracted/render.nix`) uses this
copy too. `_redact` is reserved syntax: `isReserved` holds for any set with the
key, valid or not, and a reserved set that is no reference is refused through
`sealed`, judged after null attributes are dropped.

### Why refusals never print the value

A literal assigned where a reference belongs is almost always the secret itself.
The module system prints any definition that fails a type's `check`. So
`redacted` and `maybeRedacted` accept everything in `check` and refuse in
`merge`, through `sealed`. Its message names the option and never the value.

Two consequences:

- `either redacted x` or `oneOf [redacted ...]` always picks `redacted`, because
  its `check` is always true. Use `maybeRedacted x` instead.
- tryEval drops throw messages, so `checks/redact/messages.nix` evaluates each
  refusal in a dummy-store `nix-instantiate`. The sentinel exists only at build
  time and reaches the probe as an argument. It cannot appear in the probe
  source, so finding it in the output can only mean a leak.

### Types

- `types.redacted` is sealed. It takes a reference, or a concat with one.
- `types.maybeRedacted t` takes a value of `t`, as visible cleartext, or
  anything `redacted` takes. For any other value it calls `redacted.merge`, so a
  change to `redacted` reaches it. A value carrying `_redact` always goes to
  `redacted`, so `t = attrsOf ...` never absorbs a reference as cleartext.
  Errors raised by `t`'s own merge belong to `t`; the values in them were
  declared cleartext.
- `types.environment` is `attrsOf` a type that also takes null. A name that
  `lib/redact/classify.nix` flags as secret requires `redacted`. Any other name
  takes `maybeRedacted str`. Either also takes a `secretFile` value, for
  `ai.services`. Names must be shell identifiers, even when the value is null. A
  null defined beside a value is refused as a conflict, without the value. null
  drops the definition and `assign` emits nothing for it, so an inherited
  variable is not unset; removing one is up to the consumer's launcher.
- `types.secretFile` takes what `redacted` takes and tags it; see Secret files.
- `types.orSecretFile t` takes a value of `t` or a tagged value, for a field
  `ai.services` delivers. A tagged and an untagged definition of one option are
  refused together rather than tagging the other.

### Secret files: path delivery

Some settings want the path of a file holding the secret, not the value: CPA
Manager Plus's key files, CLIProxyAPI's `server.tls.key`. The option definer
types such an option `types.secretFile`; the consumer still writes
`redact.file`, `redact.command` or `redact.concat`. Its merge refuses what
`redacted` refuses and tags the rest as `{_redact.asFile = <reference>;}`; a
tagged definition passes unchanged, so one secretFile option can feed another.

Only the `ai.services` launcher delivers a tagged value
(`packages/ai-module/docs/DESIGN.md`, Services): it writes the value to a 0600
file in the service's runtime directory and passes that path where the value
would go. A `redact.file` reference is copied too, so every secret file has one
mode, owner and lifetime. `filePaths` sees through the tag, so restart triggers
and provider ordering come from the reference. Anywhere else a tagged value
fails evaluation: `sealed` says only an `ai.services` launcher delivers it, so
`assign` and `redacted` never hand a path to a consumer that takes the value.

### Delivery: `assign`, a function and not a type

`assign {pkgs; option; variable; value; export ? false;}` emits launch-time
shell. The consumer picks `variable`, so no user-facing env-name option exists.
Literals are shell-escaped, and null emits nothing. A reference or concat
becomes one call:

```sh
VAR="$(<reader> <option> <kind> <source> ...)" || exit 1
```

`|| exit 1` aborts even in a caller without errexit, and the runtime check runs
its consumers under `set +o errexit`. The reader's argv carries only the label,
the kinds (`literal`, `file`, `command`), the paths and the literal parts. The
value travels on stdout. Command substitution drops trailing newlines of the
joined value.

### The reader

`reader.nix` is the one reader, a strict `writeShellApplication`. For each
reference it aborts on a missing file, a directory, an unreadable file, an empty
value, a NUL byte, or a failing command. It strips trailing newlines. A command
runs with stderr discarded, and its output is never echoed. Each failure prints
`<option>: <reason>` and exits 1 before anything reaches stdout.

The reader keeps the caller's PATH for the command it runs, so it renders
`export PATH="$PATH"` under `nounset`. A launcher started with no PATH at all,
as Claude Code's MCP `env` can do, aborts at the reader. Set PATH in such a
launcher before `assign` runs.

The directory test comes first, because `-e` and `-r` are both true for a
readable directory. A NUL from a command can stop the read early, so it may
surface as "command failed" rather than "NUL byte". Either way the reader
aborts.
